guide_description: Three days organised around Kyoto's geography rather than its highlight list, since the city's sights sit in tight clusters separated by long bus rides. Day one walks the stone lanes of Southern Higashiyama into Gion, day two stays in Arashiyama on the western edge, and day three starts before dawn at Fushimi Inari and works north along the Kamo. Two of the three days end at a river, which is when Kyoto is at its best.

days.cluster_tagline: A hillside temple on stilts, preserved stone lanes, and the wooden teahouse district after dark
days.neighborhood_description: The strip of hillside running north from Kiyomizu-dera to Yasaka Shrine holds the densest concentration of preserved streetscape in Kyoto, protected by strict height and signage rules that keep the wires buried and the buildings low. Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka are the two stepped lanes threading through it. At the northern end the district flattens into Gion, the traditional entertainment quarter, where Hanamikoji and the Shirakawa canal are the two streets worth walking slowly.

morning.unesco_designation: Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)
morning.notes: The temple has long opened at 6:00, earlier than almost anything else in Kyoto, and arriving in that first hour is the difference between a mountain temple and a queue. The wooden stage projects thirteen metres over the hillside on a joinery frame built without nails, and the view back over the city is best in early light. Follow the path down to the Otowa waterfall and the three streams, then leave by the Sannenzaka steps rather than doubling back the way you came. Crowds here peak during cherry blossom in early April and maple season in the second half of November, when evening illuminations also run; check the temple's own calendar for those dates.

afternoon.notes: Founded in 1606 by Nene in memory of her husband Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and quiet in a way its neighbours two hundred metres downhill are not. The strength here is the garden: a dry landscape section, a pond garden attributed to Kobori Enshu, and a bamboo path at the back that most visitors to Arashiyama's famous grove would find more atmospheric. The Otama-ya mausoleum holds some of the finest surviving Momoyama lacquerwork. Eat lunch on the walk up through Ninenzaka, where the yudofu and soba shops are unremarkable and convenient.

evening.notes: Walk Hanamikoji south from Shijo as the lanterns come on, then double back and follow the Shirakawa canal, which is the quieter and more attractive half of the district and where the willows overhang the water. Private alleys off Hanamikoji have been closed to visitors with fines attached after years of harassment of geiko and maiko; stay on the public streets and do not photograph anyone in costume without asking. Most of the ochaya are introduction-only and closed to walk-ins, so treat the evening as a walk rather than a night out. Gion Matsuri fills all of July, with the main processions on the 17th and 24th, and accommodation across the city books out months ahead for it.

if_time_permits.notes: Open around the clock and free, which makes it the natural hinge between the Higashiyama lanes and Gion. The dance stage hung with hundreds of lantern boxes, each paid for by a local business, is lit after dark and photographs better than it looks in daylight. Maruyama Park behind it is Kyoto's most popular hanami spot, with a weeping cherry lit at night in early April and a crowd to match.

Head temple of Jodo-shu Pure Land Buddhism, entered through the largest wooden temple gate in Japan, a 1621 structure that dwarfs everything around it. The scale is the point: the main hall, the stone stairways, and a 70-tonne bell that takes seventeen monks to ring at New Year. Far fewer visitors than Kiyomizu-dera despite sitting fifteen minutes away.

days.cluster_tagline: A Zen pond garden, a bamboo path best walked at dawn, and the Katsura river at dusk
days.neighborhood_description: Arashiyama sits at the western edge of the Kyoto basin where the Katsura river comes out of the mountains, and it has been a retreat for the Kyoto aristocracy since the Heian period. The core around Tenryu-ji and the bamboo grove is intensely busy by mid-morning; the Sagano hills immediately north hold a scattering of small temples that stay quiet all day. The whole day is walkable end to end, which is unusual for Kyoto.

morning.activity_title: Tenryu-ji and the Sagano Bamboo Grove
morning.unesco_designation: Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)
morning.notes: The bamboo grove is free, always open, and completely different before 8:00 than after, so do it first and let the temple opening time set the rest of the morning. Tenryu-ji's Sogenchi garden survives essentially as Muso Soseki laid it out in the fourteenth century, borrowing the Arashiyama hills as background, and the garden ticket is sold separately from the buildings. Take the north gate exit, which puts you directly onto the bamboo path with the crowds walking the other way. The temple runs a shojin ryori vegetarian lunch on site; reserve ahead if you want it.

afternoon.notes: The private villa and hillside garden of Denjiro Okochi, a silent-film era jidaigeki star who spent thirty years building it. Admission is higher than most temples and includes matcha and a sweet at the teahouse on the way out, which is why the crowd thins here and almost nobody who walks the bamboo path continues the extra two hundred metres to the gate. The circuit climbs to a viewpoint over the Hozu gorge and the city beyond. Best in mid-November when the maples turn, and genuinely peaceful even then.

walk_to_next.to: Togetsukyo Bridge and the Katsura riverfront

evening.activity_title: Togetsukyo Bridge and the Katsura riverfront
evening.notes: The moon-crossing bridge has spanned this stretch of the Katsura in some form since the ninth century, and the current concrete-cored structure keeps the old wooden railings. Cross to the south bank and walk upstream for the view back toward the gorge with the hills closing in, which is where the light does the work at the end of the day. Rental boats operate on the river in the warmer months and the last ones go out well before dusk. Most of Arashiyama shuts early, so plan dinner back in central Kyoto; the JR Sagano line to Kyoto Station runs about fifteen minutes.

if_time_permits.notes: The Golden Pavilion is the most photographed building in Japan and the visit is a one-way loop of about forty minutes with no interior access, so an hour covers it fully. The gold leaf reflected in Kyoko-chi pond works best in morning light or after fresh snow, and the current structure dates to a 1955 reconstruction after an arson that Mishima built a novel around. Getting here from Arashiyama takes roughly thirty to forty minutes by Kyoto City Bus 59 or by the Randen tram with a change, so treat it as a substitution for the afternoon rather than an addition to the day.

walk_from_main_route.from: Tenryu-ji and the Sagano Bamboo Grove

if_time_permits.notes: A small hillside temple on Mount Ogura with a thatched gate, a two-storey pagoda, and a steep moss-and-maple approach that turns spectacular in late autumn. It sits ten minutes past the point where the Arashiyama crowds stop walking, and on a weekday you may have the upper terrace and its view over the Sagano plain to yourself. Pair it with Gio-ji and Nison-in nearby if you want a full afternoon of small temples.

days.cluster_name: Fushimi Inari and the Kamo Riverfront
days.cluster_tagline: Ten thousand torii before breakfast, a Zen maple valley, and dinner on a lantern-lit alley
days.neighborhood_description: South Kyoto runs along the Keihan line, with Fushimi Inari and Tofuku-ji two stops apart and both within walking distance of each other along quiet residential streets. North of them the city tightens into the central grid, where Ponto-cho and Kiyamachi run parallel to the Kamo river and hold most of Kyoto's evening life in an area a few blocks wide.

morning.notes: The shrine grounds are open at all hours and free, which makes a 7:00 arrival both possible and the single best piece of timing advice in Kyoto. The torii tunnels run about four kilometres up Mount Inari and take roughly two hours round trip to the summit; the Yotsutsuji junction at the halfway point gives the city view and is where most people sensibly turn back. Every gate was paid for by a business, with the donor and date carved on the reverse, so the walk back down reads as a directory of Japanese commerce. Head shrine of Inari and the origin of some 30,000 branch shrines nationwide.

afternoon.notes: One of the great Zen monasteries of Kyoto, founded in 1236, with a sanmon gate that is the oldest of its kind in Japan. The Tsutenkyo bridge crosses a valley of two thousand maples and is the reason this temple is famous, which means late November brings genuine congestion and a separate ticketed entry system; every other month it is calm. The Hojo garden by Mirei Shigemori, laid out in 1939 with moss set into a checkerboard of cut stone, is the most interesting modern Japanese garden in the city and is ticketed separately. Lunch options nearby are thin, so eat around Fushimi Inari's approach street before walking over.

evening.notes: Take the Keihan line from Tofukuji station to Gion-Shijo, about eight minutes, rather than making the walk. Ponto-cho is a single alley barely two metres wide running five blocks between Shijo and Sanjo, lantern-lit and lined with restaurants at every price point from standing yakitori to kaiseki behind unmarked doors. From May through September many of the restaurants on the river side open kawayuka, wooden platforms built out over the Kamo, and reserving one is worth the premium on a warm night. If everything is full, the Kamo riverbank below is where half of Kyoto sits in summer with convenience store beer, evenly spaced by unspoken agreement.

if_time_permits.notes: A 120-metre wooden hall from 1266 holding 1,001 gilded Kannon statues in ranked rows, with twenty-eight guardian deities standing in front of them. Photography is prohibited inside, which turns out to be the making of the place. Each of the thousand standing figures was individually carved and no two faces match, and the tradition holds that you will find someone you know among them. Twenty minutes on foot from Tofuku-ji and directly on the way back into the centre.

Five covered blocks of food stalls that have supplied Kyoto's kitchens for four centuries, running west from Teramachi. Pickles, tofu skin, dashi, knives, and a growing proportion of stalls aimed squarely at visitors, which the older shopkeepers will tell you about at length. Most stalls close by early evening, so it works better as a late-afternoon detour on the way to Ponto-cho than as a dinner plan. Eating while walking is discouraged and several stalls provide a counter for exactly that reason.
